UNIT 5: PLATE TECTONICS
Strand 1: The Physical Environment.

KEY THEME
- Plate tectonics is the study of tectonic plates and how they interact at their boundaries.
- Plates can diverge (move apart), converge (collide) or slide past each other.
- This drives major geological processes: earthquakes, volcanic activity, mountain building, and the creation and destruction of ocean basins.

LEARNING OUTCOMES (1.1)
- Name and locate all the Earth's main plates.
- Describe how convection currents work and how they lead to plate movement.
- Describe and explain the processes at constructive, transform and destructive plate boundaries.
- Links to Unit 9: The Rock Cycle.

KEY TERMS
- Moho line: the boundary between the Earth's crust and the mantle.
- Lithosphere: the rigid outer layer of the Earth, made up of the crust and the uppermost part of the mantle.
- Asthenosphere: the softer, semi-fluid layer of the mantle just below the lithosphere.
- Fault: a break in the rocks of the crust along which rocks on either side have moved past each other.
- Strike-slip fault: a fault where two blocks of crust move past each other horizontally, not up or down. If the block on the opposite side moves to the right it is a right-lateral strike-slip fault; if to the left, a left-lateral strike-slip fault.
- Shear stress: a force that makes the crust move sideways, especially where plates slide past each other at transform boundaries.
- Constructive (divergent) boundary: where two plates move away from each other.
- Mid-ocean ridge: an underwater mountain range formed by plate tectonics.
- Volcanic islands: islands formed by eruptions of volcanoes on the ocean floor.
- Destructive (convergent) boundary: where two plates move towards each other and collide.
- Subduction: the process by which one plate moves under another and sinks into the mantle.
- Subduction zone: where one plate slides under another at a destructive boundary.
- Ocean trench: a long, deep depression in the ocean bed, running parallel to a plate boundary and marking the subduction zone.
- Slab pull: the pulling of oceanic plates down into the mantle due to gravity.
- Plate deformation: the bending, stretching or breaking of plates as they move and interact.

STRUCTURE OF THE EARTH (FIGURES 5.1 AND 5.2)
- Crust: the solid outermost layer. Two types:
- Continental crust: makes up the land and forms continental plates. 40-70 km thick; less dense; mainly silica and aluminium (SIAL); main rock granite; found on continents and continental shelves.
- Oceanic crust: lies beneath the oceans and forms oceanic plates. 6-12 km thick; denser; mainly silica and magnesium (SIMA); main rock basalt; found in ocean basins.
- Mantle: beneath the crust; a thick layer of hot, dense rock rich in iron and magnesium.
- Lithosphere: the crust plus the upper part of the mantle - a rigid, solid shell about 100 km thick, broken into sections called tectonic plates.
- Asthenosphere: just below the lithosphere; part of the upper mantle where rock is hotter and partially melted, so it is weak and flows very slowly. This lets the lithosphere move over it, driving plate movement.
- Outer core: a liquid layer of iron and nickel.
- Inner core: a solid ball of iron and nickel at the very centre.

CONVECTION CURRENTS AND PLATE MOVEMENT (FIGURE 5.3)
- Convection currents in the mantle move the tectonic plates.
- Intense heat from the core makes molten rock in the mantle hotter, so it rises towards the crust.
- When it reaches the upper mantle and crust it cools, becomes denser and sinks back towards the core.
- As it sinks it heats up again, and the cycle repeats over and over.
- Convection currents act like a conveyor belt beneath the lithosphere, dragging plates along.
- Friction and movement of mantle material push or pull plates in different directions: they separate (diverge), collide (converge) or slide past each other (transform).
- Convection currents and plate movement are responsible for forming mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes.

PLATE BOUNDARIES (FIGURE 5.4)
- Plate boundaries are where plates diverge, converge and transform.
- There are eight major plates and many smaller ones. Main plates named: Pacific, North American, South American, Eurasian, African, Indo-Australian, Nazca and Antarctic.
- Tectonic forces: tension (pulling apart), shearing (sideways), compression (pushing together).

1. CONSTRUCTIVE (DIVERGENT) PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Two plates move away from each other.
- Tension causes the crust to stretch and thin - this is plate deformation.
- Magma rises through fissures (cracks) in the stretched crust. When it cools and hardens it forms new crust.
- They are called 'constructive' because they build new crust. New land is created where oceanic plates separate and continental plates split.
FORMATION OF MID-OCEAN RIDGES AND OCEAN BASINS
- Under the oceans, divergent boundaries create mid-ocean ridges: long underwater mountain ranges where magma rises, cools and forms new oceanic crust.
- This process is sea-floor spreading. It slowly widens ocean basins and pushes continents apart.
- As plates diverge, crust thins and fissures form; magma rises, cools rapidly, hardens and builds up into a ridge.
- Rock on the sea floor is youngest at the ridge and gets progressively older further away.
- Example: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the Eurasian and North American Plates separate. The Atlantic Ocean basin is widening by about 4 cm per year. Iceland is a volcanic island on the ridge.
CREATION OF RIFT VALLEYS
- On land, divergent boundaries stretch and thin the crust, forming rift valleys, e.g. the East African Rift.
- Magma rises through fissures in continental crust to form volcanoes, e.g. Mount Kilimanjaro.
- Rift valleys can become so deep and wide that they fill with water, forming new seas or even oceans. They are the first step in the breakup of continents.
- How a rift valley forms (Figure 5.8): (a) tensional forces pull the crust apart and normal faults form; (b) the central block between the faults drops down as the crust thins and subsides; (c) a fully formed rift valley with steep sides and a sunken floor develops.
- Afar Region, Ethiopia: sits on the junction of three plates - Arabian, Nubian and Somalian (the Afar Triple Junction). The Arabian Plate is being pulled north-east and the Somalian Plate eastward. Eventually the crust will collapse and a new inlet of the sea will form.
EARTHQUAKES AND VOLCANOES AT DIVERGENT BOUNDARIES
- Earthquakes are common but generally less severe than at convergent boundaries; usually shallow.
- Upwelling magma causes volcanic activity, especially along mid-ocean ridges, forming new crust and sea-floor volcanic features. Volcanoes are less explosive. Example: volcanic islands like Iceland (places on the Iceland map: Krafla, Thingvellir, Reykjavik).
- Summary table: movement apart; new crust created; earthquakes yes, usually shallow; volcanoes yes, less explosive; examples Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift.

2. TRANSFORM PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Also called sliding plate boundaries. Two plates slide past each other sideways rather than colliding or separating.
- Land is neither created nor destroyed.
- Plates move in opposite directions along a fault line, or sometimes in the same direction at different speeds.
- Example: the San Andreas Fault, California. The Pacific Plate moves at about 5 cm per year past the North American Plate, which moves at about 1 cm per year. Cities nearby: San Francisco and Los Angeles.
- Sideways movement creates shear stress. As rocks are forced sideways over a large area, the crust breaks and shatters along the fault, making the ground bend, crack and shift.
- The plates do not slide smoothly: they get stuck and stress builds up. Eventually they slip and break free, causing an earthquake.
- No volcanic activity, because no magma is produced or pushed to the surface.
- Earthquakes usually occur close to the surface and are often strong and violent.
- Summary table: movement horizontal (side-by-side); crust neither created nor destroyed; earthquakes yes, often large and shallow; volcanoes no; example San Andreas Fault.

3. DESTRUCTIVE (CONVERGENT) PLATE BOUNDARIES
- Two plates move towards each other and collide. Results depend on the crust type (oceanic or continental), but always involve dramatic reshaping of the surface.
- Slab pull drives this movement, especially at subduction zones where dense oceanic plates sink beneath less dense plates. Gravity acting on the sinking plate creates a downward pull that drags the rest of the plate behind it. Slab pull is the main driver of plate motion.
(A) OCEANIC-CONTINENTAL COLLISION (FIGURE 5.15)
- Dense oceanic plate (e.g. Nazca Plate) meets less dense continental plate (e.g. South American Plate).
- Convection currents move the plates together; slab pull drags the oceanic plate beneath the continental plate - subduction.
- This creates deep ocean trenches (e.g. the Peru-Chile Trench) and can trigger powerful earthquakes and volcanic eruptions.
- The subducting plate carries mineral-rich sediments into the mantle. As it sinks and heats up, water is released, lowering the melting point of the rock above. This causes partial melting and forms magma, which rises through the continental crust and erupts as volcanoes.
- Repeated eruptions build volcanic mountain ranges. A chain of volcanoes forms parallel to the subduction zone, e.g. the Andes volcanic arc.
- The sinking plate scrapes and compresses the edge of the continental crust, making it thicken and sometimes fold. This pushes the crust upward - mountain building, e.g. the Andes in South America.
(B) CONTINENTAL-CONTINENTAL COLLISION (FIGURE 5.16)
- Both plates are too light to be pushed under each other easily, so there is very little subduction.
- Intense pressure makes rocks bend and fold: upfolds are anticlines, downfolds are synclines. Overall the crust is forced upwards, beginning fold mountain ranges, e.g. the Alps (African Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate).
- Magma can intrude into gaps between folds and cool slowly to form new rock underground (volcanic intrusions).
- Little volcanic activity.
(C) OCEANIC-OCEANIC COLLISION (FIGURE 5.18)
- Convection currents moving in the same direction can make two oceanic plates collide.
- Example: near Japan, the denser Pacific Plate is forced beneath the Eurasian Plate (subduction), creating a deep trench - the Japan Trench.
- The sinking plate melts, creating silica- and gas-rich magma that rises through the overlying plate, causing eruptions on the sea floor.
- Over time a chain of volcanic islands forms parallel to the subduction zone - an island arc, e.g. Japan's volcanic arc.
- Powerful earthquakes happen when plates suddenly slip; sea-floor earthquakes can trigger tsunamis.
- In the summary: the older, denser plate subducts beneath the other.
CONVERGENT BOUNDARY SUMMARY TABLE
- Oceanic-continental: Nazca Plate under South American Plate - Andes Mountains and Peru-Chile Trench; volcanoes, deep trenches, mountains.
- Oceanic-oceanic: Pacific Plate under Eurasian Plate - Japanese Islands and deep trenches; island arcs, deep trenches.
- Continental-continental: African Plate with Eurasian Plate - the Alps; huge mountain ranges.
- Earthquakes at convergent boundaries are often powerful, including deep earthquakes in subduction zones.

EXAM SKILLS
- SEC HL Sample Paper 1, Q2(a)(i): draw a labelled diagram of a destructive plate boundary showing directions of plate movement, convection currents, an oceanic trench and slab pull. Sample diagram labels: oceanic trench, plate movement arrows, slab pull, cooler magma, hot magma, convection currents.
- SEC OL Sample Paper 1, Q2(a): example of a mid-ocean ridge = Mid-Atlantic Ridge; it forms at a constructive plate boundary; diagram showing two oceanic plates moving apart (North American and Eurasian), the mid-ocean ridge, rising magma and convection currents.

DIAGRAMS DESCRIBED IN WORDS
- Convection currents: a cross-section with the core at the bottom; arrows show hot magma rising from the core, spreading out under the plates, cooling and sinking back down in loops; plates on top are dragged apart where currents rise and together where they sink.
- Mid-ocean ridge: two oceanic plates with arrows pointing away from each other; magma rising up through a central crack to form a ridge on the sea floor; convection current loops in the mantle beneath.
- Oceanic-continental subduction: an oceanic plate sloping down beneath a continental plate; a trench at the junction; slab pull arrow on the sinking slab; magma rising from the melting zone to volcanoes on the continent; mountains on the continental edge.

rows.prompt: What is the solid outermost layer of the Earth called?
rows.explanation: The crust forms the solid outermost layer.

rows.prompt: The Moho line is the boundary between:
options: The mantle and the outer core
rows.explanation: The Moho line separates the crust from the mantle.

rows.prompt: The lithosphere is made up of:
options: The crust and the uppermost mantle
rows.explanation: The lithosphere is the rigid crust plus upper mantle, about 100 km thick.

rows.prompt: Why can plates move over the asthenosphere?
options: It is solid iron and nickel
It is hot, partly melted and flows slowly
It is colder than the crust
rows.explanation: The asthenosphere is weak and semi-fluid, so the lithosphere moves over it.

rows.prompt: What is the outer core made of?
rows.explanation: The outer core is liquid iron and nickel; the inner core is solid.

rows.prompt: Which is true of oceanic crust compared with continental crust?
options: It is thicker and less dense
It is mainly silica and aluminium
rows.explanation: Oceanic crust is 6-12 km thick, denser, mainly basalt (SIMA).

rows.prompt: Continental crust is mainly made of silica and aluminium. This is known as:
rows.explanation: Continental crust is SIAL; oceanic crust is SIMA.

rows.prompt: How thick is continental crust?
rows.explanation: Continental crust is 40-70 km thick.

rows.prompt: What causes convection currents in the mantle?
options: Intense heat from the Earth's core
rows.explanation: Heat from the core makes mantle rock rise, cool and sink in a cycle.

rows.prompt: In a convection current, mantle material near the crust:
rows.explanation: Cooling material becomes denser and sinks back towards the core.

rows.prompt: Convection currents act like a ______ beneath the lithosphere.
rows.explanation: They drag the plates along like a conveyor belt.

rows.prompt: How many major tectonic plates are there?
rows.explanation: There are eight major plates and many smaller ones.

rows.prompt: At a constructive plate boundary, plates:
rows.explanation: Constructive (divergent) boundaries are where plates move apart.

rows.prompt: Which tectonic force stretches and thins the crust at divergent boundaries?
rows.explanation: Tension pulls the crust apart, stretching and thinning it.

rows.prompt: The process where new oceanic crust forms at a ridge and widens the ocean is:
rows.explanation: Sea-floor spreading widens ocean basins and pushes continents apart.

rows.prompt: The Atlantic Ocean basin is widening by approximately:
rows.explanation: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge widens the Atlantic about 4 cm a year.

rows.prompt: Where is the youngest rock on the sea floor found?
rows.explanation: Rock is youngest at the ridge and older further away.

rows.prompt: Which plates separate at the Mid-Atlantic Ridge?
rows.explanation: The Eurasian and North American Plates separate there.

rows.prompt: Which is an example of a rift valley?
rows.explanation: The East African Rift forms where continental crust stretches and thins.

rows.prompt: Which three plates meet in Ethiopia's Afar Region?
rows.explanation: Afar sits on the junction of the Arabian, Nubian and Somalian plates.

rows.prompt: In rift valley formation, what happens to the central block between faults?
options: It is pushed up into a fold
It drops down as the crust thins
rows.explanation: The central block subsides between normal faults to form the valley floor.

rows.prompt: At a transform boundary, crust is:
rows.explanation: Plates slide past each other; land is neither created nor destroyed.

rows.prompt: At the San Andreas Fault, the Pacific Plate moves at about:
rows.explanation: The Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm/year; the North American Plate about 1 cm/year.

rows.prompt: The sideways force at a transform boundary is called:
rows.explanation: Sideways movement creates shear stress.

rows.prompt: Why are there no volcanoes at transform boundaries?
options: The crust there is too thick
No magma is produced or pushed to the surface
rows.explanation: No magma is produced, so there is no volcanic activity.

rows.prompt: When one plate sinks beneath another into the mantle, this is called:
rows.explanation: Subduction happens at destructive (convergent) boundaries.

rows.prompt: Slab pull is caused by:
options: Gravity acting on the sinking plate
rows.explanation: Gravity pulls the dense sinking slab down, dragging the plate behind it.

rows.prompt: At an oceanic-continental boundary, why does magma form?
options: The continental plate is pulled apart
Water released from the sinking plate lowers the melting point
The plates slide past each other
rows.explanation: Released water lowers the melting point of rock above, causing partial melting.

rows.prompt: Which trench forms where the Nazca Plate subducts under the South American Plate?
rows.explanation: Subduction of the Nazca Plate creates the Peru-Chile Trench.

rows.prompt: The Alps were formed by the collision of which plates?
rows.explanation: The African Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate formed the Alps.

rows.prompt: Why is there very little subduction when two continental plates collide?
options: Both plates are too light to sink
There is no convection below them
rows.explanation: Continental crust is light, so neither plate is easily pushed under.

rows.prompt: An oceanic-oceanic collision forms a chain of volcanic islands called:
rows.explanation: E.g. Japan's volcanic arc forms parallel to the subduction zone.

rows.prompt: Name the layers of the Earth from the outside in, with one fact about each.
rows.model_answer: Crust: the solid outer layer, continental or oceanic. Mantle: thick hot, dense rock rich in iron and magnesium. Outer core: liquid iron and nickel. Inner core: a solid ball of iron and nickel at the centre.

rows.prompt: Compare continental crust and oceanic crust (thickness, density, rock type).
rows.model_answer: Continental crust is 40-70 km thick, less dense, mainly silica and aluminium (SIAL) and mainly granite. Oceanic crust is 6-12 km thick, denser, mainly silica and magnesium (SIMA) and mainly basalt.

rows.prompt: Explain in your own words how convection currents move tectonic plates.
rows.model_answer: Heat from the core makes molten mantle rock rise towards the crust. There it cools, becomes denser and sinks back down, where it heats again and the cycle repeats. These currents act like a conveyor belt, dragging plates apart, together or past each other.

rows.prompt: Explain how a mid-ocean ridge forms, naming an example.
rows.model_answer: At a divergent boundary, two oceanic plates move apart and tension thins the crust, forming fissures. Magma rises through the fissures, cools and hardens to form new crust, which builds up into an underwater mountain range. Example: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, where the Eurasian and North American Plates separate.

rows.prompt: Describe the three stages in the formation of a rift valley (describe the diagram in words).
rows.model_answer: (a) Tension pulls the crust apart and normal faults form. (b) The central block between the faults drops down as the crust thins and subsides. (c) A rift valley with steep sides and a sunken floor forms, e.g. the East African Rift.

rows.prompt: Explain why earthquakes happen at transform boundaries like the San Andreas Fault.
rows.model_answer: The plates slide sideways past each other, creating shear stress. They do not move smoothly, so they get stuck and stress builds up. When they suddenly slip and break free, an earthquake happens, often shallow and violent.

rows.prompt: What is slab pull and why is it important?
rows.model_answer: Slab pull is the pulling of a dense oceanic plate down into the mantle by gravity at a subduction zone. The sinking slab drags the rest of the plate behind it, making slab pull the main driver of plate motion.

rows.prompt: Compare the features formed at the three types of convergent boundary, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Oceanic-continental: volcanoes, deep trenches and mountains, e.g. the Andes and Peru-Chile Trench. Oceanic-oceanic: island arcs and deep trenches, e.g. Japan and the Japan Trench. Continental-continental: huge fold mountain ranges, e.g. the Alps.

rows.prompt: Examine the processes at work at constructive (divergent) plate boundaries, with reference to examples you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: At constructive plate boundaries, two plates move away from each other. This is driven by convection currents in the mantle: heat from the core makes molten rock rise, cool near the crust and sink again, dragging plates apart like a conveyor belt. As the plates pull apart, tension stretches and thins the crust; this is plate deformation. Fissures open and magma rises through them, cooling and hardening to form new crust, so these boundaries are called constructive. Under the ocean this creates mid-ocean ridges, long underwater mountain ranges. This process is sea-floor spreading, which widens ocean basins and pushes continents apart. Rock is youngest along the ridge and gets older further away. At the Mid-Atlantic Ridge the Eurasian and North American Plates separate and the Atlantic widens by about 4 cm per year. Upwelling magma along the ridge forms volcanic islands such as Iceland, and volcanoes here are less explosive. On land, the crust stretches to form rift valleys, such as the East African Rift. Normal faults form and the central block drops down to make a steep-sided valley. Magma rising through fissures forms volcanoes like Mount Kilimanjaro. In Afar, Ethiopia, the Arabian, Nubian and Somalian plates are pulling apart and a new sea inlet will eventually form. Earthquakes are common but usually shallow and less severe.
rows.marking_scheme: Name process (e.g. sea-floor spreading/rifting) 2m. Named example 2m. Examination: 13 SRPs x 2 marks. Credit convection currents, tension, plate deformation, fissures, magma/new crust, mid-ocean ridge, sea-floor spreading, rock age, 4 cm/yr, Iceland, rift valley stages, Kilimanjaro, Afar, earthquakes. Max 30 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain the processes that occur at destructive (convergent) plate boundaries, with reference to examples you have studied. (30 marks)
rows.model_answer: At destructive boundaries two plates move towards each other and collide. Slab pull, where gravity drags a dense oceanic plate into the mantle, is the main driver. Where the oceanic Nazca Plate meets the continental South American Plate, the denser oceanic plate is subducted. This creates a deep ocean trench, the Peru-Chile Trench, and triggers powerful earthquakes. As the plate sinks and heats, water is released, lowering the melting point of the rock above. Partial melting forms magma, which rises through the continental crust and erupts, building the Andes volcanic arc parallel to the subduction zone. The sinking plate also compresses the edge of the continent, thickening and folding it upwards to form the Andes Mountains. Where two oceanic plates collide, such as the Pacific Plate subducting under the Eurasian Plate near Japan, a deep trench forms, the Japan Trench. Silica- and gas-rich magma rises to form an island arc, Japan's volcanic arc. Sudden slips cause earthquakes, and sea-floor earthquakes can trigger tsunamis. Where two continental plates collide, such as the African and Eurasian Plates, both are too light to subduct. Intense pressure folds the rocks into anticlines and synclines and forces the crust upwards to form fold mountains, the Alps. Magma can intrude between the folds and cool slowly underground.
rows.marking_scheme: Name process (subduction/folding) 2m. Named example 2m. Explanation: 13 SRPs x 2 marks. Credit slab pull, subduction, trench, water/melting point, magma, volcanic arc, compression/folding, Andes, oceanic-oceanic (Japan, island arc, tsunami), continental-continental (Alps, anticlines/synclines, intrusions). Max 30 marks.

rows.prompt: With the aid of a labelled diagram, explain what convection currents are and describe their role in the movement of tectonic plates. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Diagram (in words): a cross-section with the core at the bottom, the mantle above it and two plates on top. Curved arrows show hot magma rising from the core, spreading out beneath the plates, cooling and sinking back down. Plates are labelled with arrows moving apart above rising currents. Explanation: Intense heat from the core makes molten rock in the mantle hotter and less dense, so it rises towards the crust. Near the crust it cools, becomes denser and sinks back towards the core, where it heats up again and the cycle repeats. These currents act like a conveyor belt beneath the lithosphere, dragging plates along. Friction pushes or pulls the plates so they separate, collide or slide past each other. The plates move over the asthenosphere, a hot, partly melted layer that flows slowly. Convection currents are responsible for forming mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes.
rows.marking_scheme: Diagram 4m (graded: core, mantle, plates, current arrows labelled). Explanation: 8 SRPs x 2 marks. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: Explain the processes at work at transform plate boundaries, with reference to a named example. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: At a transform, or sliding, plate boundary, two plates slide past each other sideways instead of colliding or moving apart, so crust is neither created nor destroyed. They move in opposite directions along a fault line, or in the same direction at different speeds. At the San Andreas Fault in California, the Pacific Plate moves about 5 cm per year past the North American Plate, which moves about 1 cm per year. The sideways movement creates shear stress. The crust breaks and shatters along the fault, making the ground bend, crack and shift. The plates do not slide smoothly; they get stuck and stress builds up. When they suddenly slip, an earthquake occurs. These earthquakes are close to the surface and often strong and violent. There is no volcanic activity because no magma is produced.
rows.marking_scheme: Named example 2m. Explanation: 9 SRPs x 2 marks. Max 20 marks.

rows.prompt: (i) Name the boundary type found at each of the following: the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the San Andreas Fault, the Andes. (ii) Name two plates that collide and two plates that separate. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: (i) Mid-Atlantic Ridge: constructive (divergent). San Andreas Fault: transform. Andes: destructive (convergent). (ii) Collide: the Nazca Plate and the South American Plate. Separate: the Eurasian Plate and the North American Plate.
rows.marking_scheme: (i) 3 x 2m = 6m. (ii) 2 x 2m = 4m (both plates needed for each pair). Max 10 marks.
